# Pharmaceutical Cold-Chain Distribution Strategy: West & East Africa

## Executive Summary

This strategy designs a **differentiated cold-chain network for temperature-sensitive vaccines across West and East Africa**, recognizing that infrastructure, institutional capacity, regulatory environments, and seasonal constraints vary sharply by corridor. Rather than imposing a uniform approach, the framework recommends:

1. **Corridor-specific infrastructure tiers** (light, medium, heavy) based on road quality, electricity reliability, customs efficiency, and last-mile complexity
2. **Phased rollout (24 months)** prioritizing high-volume, lower-complexity corridors first; scaling to difficult routes once proven
3. **Hybrid equipment strategy**—passive cooling (containers + phase-change materials) for mature routes; powered units (solar-hybrid) for unreliable grid corridors; local partnerships for last-mile handoff
4. **Risk-stratified spoilage prevention** through temperature monitoring (real-time IoT sensors), redundant cooling, buffer stock positioning, and demand-driven pull logistics
5. **Ministry of Health (MoH) integration and institutional capacity-building** to ensure supply-side reliability and regulatory compliance

**Target outcomes (24-month horizon):**
- **Spoilage rate:** <2% network average (vs. 5–8% industry baseline in African corridors)
- **On-time delivery:** 90%+ to provincial depots (>85% to remote health centers)
- **Cold-chain integrity:** 99%+ of shipments maintain 2–8°C (or manufacturer spec) end-to-end
- **Cost efficiency:** $0.40–0.60 per dose delivered (vs. $0.80–1.50 regional average)
- **Institutional readiness:** 80%+ of MoH partner facilities achieve WHO cold-chain performance standards within 18 months
- **Sustainability:** Equipment and processes transferable to local operators; knowledge transfer embedded

---

## Part I: Diagnostic & Market Foundation

### A. West & East Africa Cold-Chain Context

#### 1. Regional Infrastructure Snapshot

**West Africa** (FRA—French-speaking regions; ENA—English-speaking):

| Corridor | Route Example | Road Quality | Electrification | Customs Efficiency | Rainy Season | Key Challenge |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| **WA-1 (High-Capacity Hub)** | Senegal → Mali, Burkina Faso | Good (60%); fair (40%) | 50–70% grid access | 24–48 hrs | Jun–Sep | Volume scale; hub management |
| **WA-2 (Coastal Tier-2)** | Côte d'Ivoire → Ghana → Togo | Fair (40%); poor (60%) | 40–60% grid | 48–72 hrs | May–Oct | Road deterioration; power cuts |
| **WA-3 (Inland Savanna)** | Burkina Faso → Niger → Mali | Poor (20%); very poor (80%) | 20–40% grid access | 72–120 hrs (very unreliable) | Jul–Sep | Sparse infrastructure; dust/heat |
| **WA-4 (Equatorial Dense)** | Nigeria → Cameroon → Gabon | Variable (30–50% good) | 30–50% grid | Highly variable | Mar–Nov | Corruption, route blocking, humidity |

**East Africa** (EAC—East African Community corridor; SEA—Southern East Africa):

| Corridor | Route Example | Road Quality | Electrification | Customs Efficiency | Dry/Wet Season | Key Challenge |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| **EA-1 (Northern Tier-1)** | Kenya (Nairobi) → Uganda, Rwanda | Good to fair (50–70%) | 60–80% grid | 24–48 hrs (reliable) | Dec–Feb (dry); Apr–May (rains) | Volume; altitude variation (cold) |
| **EA-2 (Highland-to-Lowland)** | Rwanda → Burundi → Southern Tanzania | Fair (40–50%); poor (50%) | 40–60% grid | 48–96 hrs | Variable by region | Terrain; landslide seasons |
| **EA-3 (East-Coastal)** | Tanzania (coastal) → Mozambique | Fair (40%); poor (60%) | 50–70% grid (coast); 20–40% (inland) | 48–120 hrs | Oct–Apr (rains) | Humidity; port delays; fuel scarcity |
| **EA-4 (Southern Tier)** | South Africa → Zimbabwe → Malawi | Good (70%+); fair (30%) | 80%+ grid | 12–36 hrs | Nov–Mar (rains) | Most reliable; still seasonal challenges |

**Cross-regional patterns:**

| Factor | Impact on Cold-Chain |
|---|---|
| **Road quality** | Rough roads → faster temperature cycling in vehicles; need heavier insulation; longer transit = higher spoilage risk |
| **Electricity access** | Unreliable grid → cannot rely on powered refrigerators at intermediate nodes; need passive systems or solar backup |
| **Customs delays** | 24–120+ hour dwell times → vaccines exposed; need powered containers or frequent ice replenishment for passive systems |
| **Rainy season** | Road closure risk; shortened delivery windows; humidity ingress into passive containers |
| **Fuel scarcity** | Limits powered vehicle range; availability unpredictable (prices, supply rationing); solar hybrid essential |
| **Last-mile complexity** | Health centers 50–300 km from depot; no grid; minimal staff training → need low-tech, fail-safe cooling |
| **Ambient temperature** | Sahel/equatorial zones: 30–45°C daytime; passive cooling harder; powered/solar systems needed |

---

#### 2. Vaccine Product Requirements & Spoilage Drivers

**Typical vaccine specs** (DPT, polio, measles, COVID-19 vaccines):

- **Storage requirement:** 2–8°C (standard); some newer vaccines: 15–25°C (less critical)
- **Tolerance:** Brief excursions (hours) recoverable; repeated or prolonged >8°C = potency loss (non-recoverable)
- **Shelf life:** 18–36 months at 2–8°C; dramatically shortened if exposed to heat
- **Cost per dose:** $0.50–$5.00 (depending on vaccine; COVID-19 more expensive historically)

**Spoilage drivers in African corridors:**

| Driver | Frequency | Impact | Mitigation |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Temperature excursions** (>8°C or <0°C) | 5–15% of shipments | Vaccine potency loss; unusable | Real-time monitoring; redundant cooling; buffer routes |
| **Customs dwell time** | 30–60% of total transit; unpredictable 24–120 hrs | Unrefrigerated exposure; passive systems degrade | Powered containers; frequent ice replenishment; expedited clearance |
| **Grid power failure at depot** | 20–40% frequency in Sahel; 10–20% in EA | Vaccine thaw/re-freeze cycles; degradation | Solar UPS; backup passive cooling; vaccine relocation protocols |
| **Vehicle breakdown en-route** | 2–5% of trips | Extended ambient exposure | Redundant transportation; buffer stock positioning |
| **Last-mile poor handling** | 5–10% of final-mile issues | Passive cooling breached; no re-cooling en-route | Staff training; simplified passive containers; community health worker oversight |
| **Humidity ingress** (into passive containers) | 10–20% in coastal/rainy zones | Water damage to vaccine labels; condensation → integrity risk | Silica gel; hermetic seals; desiccant monitoring; external labeling |
| **Fuel/vehicle scarcity** | Seasonal; 5–15% of deliveries delayed | Extended transit; passive cooling failure | Fuel pre-positioning; multi-modal backup; solar-powered vehicles |

**Network baseline assumption (before intervention):**
- **Spoilage rate:** 5–8% (consistent with WHO reports on African corridors)
- **Temperature excursion incidents:** 15–20% of shipments experience some out-of-range exposure
- **On-time delivery:** 70–80% (30% delay rate, mostly customs)

---

### B. Stakeholder & Institutional Landscape

#### 1. Key Actors & Incentives

| Actor | Role | Incentive | Constraint | Engagement Strategy |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **National MoH** | Demand aggregation; regulatory approval; last-mile oversight | Vaccine accessibility; budget control; political credit | Capacity (staff, funding); competing priorities | Direct partnership; capacity building; reporting dashboard |
| **Provincial Health Authorities** | Regional depot management; data reporting | Timely supply; reduced stockouts; performance metrics | Limited cold-chain skill; infrastructure gaps; funding | Training program; equipment support; KPI alignment |
| **District Health Centers** | End-user; vaccine storage & administration | Reliable supply; easy-to-use equipment; training | No electricity; minimal storage; limited staff | Ultra-simple passive containers; community health worker training |
| **Customs Authorities** | Border checkpoint clearance; documentation | Compliance; revenue/inspection efficiency | Corruption risk; bureaucratic delays; limited cold-chain awareness | Pre-clearance process; bonding; expedited lanes for health goods |
| **Transport Companies** | Vehicle provision; route management | Revenue; vehicle utilization; repeat contracts | Profitability pressure; may cut corners on maintenance/monitoring | Performance contracts; temperature tracking incentives; fuel subsidy (structured) |
| **Pharmaceutical Distributor / Manufacturer** | Supply-chain coordination; quality assurance | Market access; vaccine uptake; reputation | Cost control; risk transfer to distributor | SLAs; risk-sharing agreements; joint quality audits |
| **Cold-Chain Equipment Vendors** | Equipment supply; maintenance | Equipment sales; service contracts | Margins; local support capacity | Preferred-vendor framework; local assembly/training |

---

#### 2. Institutional Capacity Baseline

**Assumption:** Most MoH partners operating below WHO cold-chain standards.

| Institutional Aspect | Current State | Target (18 months) | Gap |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Vaccine inventory management** | Manual ledgers; high loss/waste rate (10–15%) | WHO-compliant digital tracking (OpenLMIS or equiv.); <3% loss | Training, systems, audits |
| **Cold-chain technician availability** | <1 per 50,000 pop.; minimal training | 1 per 20,000 pop.; certified maintenance skills | Recruitment, 3-month training |
| **Equipment maintenance culture** | Ad-hoc, reactive (equipment fails before repair) | Preventive maintenance schedule; <1% downtime | Spare-parts supply chain; training; accountability |
| **Temperature monitoring** | Visual check (glass thermometers); no logging | Digital min/max thermometers + IOT sensors; automated alerts | Equipment purchase; training; data protocols |
| **Emergency response protocols** | Non-existent or vague | Documented playbooks; quarterly drills; clear escalation | Protocol development; training; testing |
| **Electricity backup** | Rare (few large depots have generators) | 80% of depots have solar UPS or backup generator | Capital investment; training |
| **Staff training** | Sporadic; no certification | Structured annual curriculum; certification exam; refresher training | Training-of-trainer program; materials development |

---

## Part II: Corridor-Specific Cold-Chain Architecture

### A. Infrastructure Tier Classification & Equipment Strategy

**Framework: Assess each corridor on 4 dimensions; assign tier; specify equipment.**

#### 1. Tier Definition Matrix

| Tier | Road Quality | Grid Reliability | Customs Efficiency | Last-Mile Complexity | Typical Corridors |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| **TIER 1 (Mature)** | Good (>60%) | Reliable (>80% uptime) | 24–48 hrs | Medium (50–100 km to depot) | WA-1 (Senegal hub); EA-1 (Kenya/Uganda) |
| **TIER 2 (Developing)** | Fair (40–60%) | Moderate (50–80%) | 48–72 hrs | High (100–200 km; sparse centers) | WA-2 (Coastal); EA-2 (Highland); EA-4 (South) |
| **TIER 3 (Challenging)** | Poor (<40%) | Low (<50%) | 72–120+ hrs | Very high (sparse, remote centers) | WA-3 (Sahel); WA-4 (Nigeria/Cameroon); EA-3 (Coastal Tanzania) |
| **TIER 4 (Emergency/Seasonal)** | Variable; seasonal closure | Rare/non-existent | Unpredictable; >120 hrs | Extreme (off-road; 300+ km; minimal infrastructure) | Remote nodes in WA-3, EA-2; emergency supply routes |

---

#### 2. Equipment Strategy by Tier

**Core principle:** Match technology to corridor constraints; avoid over-specification (cost/maintenance burden) and under-specification (spoilage risk).

##### TIER 1 (Mature) Corridors: WA-1, EA-1

**Example route:** Senegal (Dakar) → Bamako (Mali) [800 km, 2–3 days]; Kenya (Nairobi) → Kampala (Uganda) [1,100 km, 2–3 days]

**Infrastructure advantages:**
- Good road; reliable grid at major depots; efficient customs (24–48 hrs)
- Existing cold-chain foundation (some equipment, basic training)

**Equipment specification:**

| Component | Technology | Rationale | Cost (per unit) | Maintenance |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **Transport container** | Insulated cold box + ice packs (passive) OR small powered cooler (500–1,000 L) | Passive sufficient; powered for high-volume bulk shipments (5,000+ doses) to hedge against delays | $300–500 (passive); $2,000–3,500 (powered) | Replace ice weekly; powered: weekly battery check |
| **Temperature monitoring** | Data logger (electronic min/max) + cloud uplink (IoT); 1 per shipment | Real-time alerts if temp exceeds range; automatic escalation | $100–200 per logger | Calibration annually |
| **Depot storage** | Refrigerated room (wall-mounted or standalone) powered by grid + solar UPS (5 kW backup) | Grid primary; solar UPS for outages (maintain 2–8°C for 8–12 hrs) | $8,000–15,000 (room); $3,000–5,000 (UPS) | Quarterly coil cleaning; annual compressor service; UPS battery replacement (3–5 yrs) |
| **Last-mile transport** | Passive insulated box (10–50 L) + ice packs OR motorcycle with small powered cooler (for 200–500 dose batches) | Passive for <8 hr trips; powered for longer routes or high-value shipments | $150–300 (passive); $1,500–2,500 (motorcycle cooler) | Ice pack replacement; vehicle maintenance |
| **Health center storage** | Vaccine freezer (if available) with solar backup OR insulated storage cabinet (passive, ice packs) + manual temperature log | Most centers: passive only; some large centers: small freezer + UPS | $1,500–2,500 (freezer + UPS); $200–400 (passive cabinet) | Ice pack replacement (weekly); freezer: annual service |

**Process & staffing:**

- **In-transit:** 1 driver + 1 temperature monitor per vehicle; driver trained on basic thermal management (avoid sun exposure, maintain ventilation)
- **Depot:** 1 cold-chain technician + 1 inventory clerk; temperature logged 3x daily (8am, 2pm, 8pm)
- **Last-mile:** Health worker (nurse, vaccination officer); trained on passive container maintenance; weekly check-in from district technician

**Spoilage risk mitigation:**

| Risk | Mitigation |
|---|---|
| Temperature excursion in-transit | Real-time monitoring; alert triggers vehicle to check/adjust; redundant ice packs (load 2x needed, 1 as backup) |
| Customs delay (>48 hrs) | Pre-clearance bonding; expedited lane for health goods; if delay occurs, move to powered cooler at checkpoint |
| Grid outage at depot | Solar UPS auto-switches; 8–12 hr backup; routine grid return within window; alert triggers manual backup cooling |
| Health center power loss | Passive cabinet + ice packs only; daily ice replenishment; inventory pulled within 48 hrs if outage extends |

**Network design:**
- Hubs at Dakar (Senegal), Bamako (Mali), Nairobi (Kenya), Kampala (Uganda)
- 2–3 regional depots (e.g., Kayes, Ségou in Mali; Kisumu, Gulu in Uganda)
- 10–15 district centers per region; served by passive shipments (weekly or bi-weekly)
- Health centers: pull supply from district center weekly (passive box; <8 hr travel time)

**Financial model (Tier 1 typical route):**
- Capital: $25K–40K per hub; $10K–15K per regional depot; $3K–5K per district center
- Operating cost: $0.08–0.12 per dose (fuel, ice packs, technician time, depreciation)
- Spoilage rate target: <1% (powered backup + monitoring + training)

---

##### TIER 2 (Developing) Corridors: WA-2, EA-2, EA-4

**Example routes:** Côte d'Ivoire (Abidjan) → Accra (Ghana) [400 km, 1–2 days]; Rwanda (Kigali) → Burundi (Bujumbura) [200 km, 4–6 hrs]; Tanzania (Dar es Salaam) → Lilongwe (Malawi) [1,200 km, 3–4 days]

**Infrastructure challenges:**
- Fair roads (40–50% deterioration risk); moderate grid (50–80% uptime); customs delays (48–72 hrs)
- Humidity (coastal EA-3 subset) or terrain/seasonal closures (EA-2)
- Mixed technician capacity (some training, inconsistent maintenance culture)

**Equipment specification:**

| Component | Technology | Rationale | Cost |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Transport container** | Insulated box (passive) + PCM (phase-change material) packs [12–18°C setpoint] instead of ice; or **hybrid passive-powered cooler** (500L, solar-charged) | PCM safer than ice (no over-cooling risk if melted; more stable temp profile); hybrid for routes with >60 hr customs risk | $400–600 (passive+PCM); $3,500–5,500 (hybrid) |
| **Temperature monitoring** | Data logger (min/max) + cellular uplink (SMS alerts); 1 per shipment | Cellular more reliable than WiFi in developing infrastructure; SMS works on basic networks | $150–250 per logger |
| **Depot storage** | Refrigerated room (grid primary) + solar hybrid UPS (10 kW; 6–8 hr backup) + manual ice-production capacity (ice maker; 50 kg/day) | Grid is primary but unreliable; solar UPS essential; ice production allows tactical cooling of passive containers during delays | $12,000–18,000 (room); $5,000–8,000 (UPS); $2,000–3,000 (ice maker) |
| **In-transit backup cooling** | Spare PCM packs (2–3x needed) + ice packs in passive containers (mix strategies); can be replenished at depot if delay | Hybrid approach: PCM for baseline, ice for tactical boost | $50–100 per shipment (consumables) |
| **Last-mile transport** | Insulated box (passive, PCM or ice) + portable solar charger (12V; for small powered coolers if available) | Most last-mile vehicles unpowered; solar charger allows 2–3 hour refresh of small cooler if needed | $300–500 (passive); $800–1,200 (with solar charger) |
| **Health center storage** | Passive insulated cabinet (PCM packs or ice) OR small solar-powered refrigerator (100–150L; standalone, no grid needed) | Some Tier 2 centers have solar potential; encourage solar-powered units for sustainability | $300–500 (passive); $2,500–4,000 (solar fridge) |

**Process & staffing:**

- **In-transit:** 1 driver + 1 cold-chain monitor (trained); route check-in twice per day (gps + temp photo via SMS)
- **Customs/depot:** Pre-positioned spare PCM/ice; protocol for replenishment if delay >24 hrs
- **Depot staff:** 1 technician (lead) + 1 assistant; daily maintenance log; ice maker operator
- **Last-mile:** Health worker + monthly district technician visit (preventive maintenance + training)

**Spoilage risk mitigation:**

| Risk | Mitigation |
|---|---|
| **Customs delay (48–72 hrs)** | Hybrid cooler on high-risk routes; if delay occurs at checkpoint, activate powered container or move to powered depot backup; pre-clearance to reduce frequency |
| **Road deterioration & temperature cycling** | PCM packs more stable than ice alone; passive container insulation sufficient if sealed well; avoid frequent opening |
| **Grid outage (50–80% uptime means failures) ** | 6–8 hr solar UPS backup; if outage extends, move vaccine to passive cabinet with ice/PCM for 48 hrs (max hold); alert MoH if >48 hr loss |
| **Humidity (coastal zones)** | Sealed passive containers; silica gel inside; desiccant packs replaced weekly; external labeling (water-resistant) |
| **Seasonal road closure** | Build buffer stock (2–4 weeks supply) at regional depot before closure window; stagger deliveries post-closure |

**Network design:**
- Hub: Abidjan (WA-2) or Dar es Salaam (EA-3); or regional split hubs for large countries
- 3–5 regional depots (e.g., Accra, Kumasi; Kigali, Butare; Dar, Mbeya)
- 8–12 district centers per region
- Health centers: pull supply every 10 days (bi-modal: passive for <8 hr; hybrid powered for >12 hr routes)

**Financial model:**
- Capital: $40K–60K per hub; $15K–25K per regional depot; $4K–7K per district center; $50K–100K for last-mile solar coolers (phased)
- Operating cost: $0.12–0.20 per dose (PCM/ice, technician, maintenance, solar/grid)
- Spoilage rate target: 1.5–2% (hybrid + monitoring + buffer stock)

---

##### TIER 3 (Challenging) Corridors: WA-3, WA-4, EA-3

**Example routes:** Burkina Faso (Ouagadougou) → Timbuktu (Mali) [1,400 km, 3–5 days, rough]; Nigeria (Lagos) → Cameroon (Yaoundé) [1,300 km, 4–5 days, variable customs]; Tanzania (Dar) → remote inland clinic [400 km, 6–10 hrs, no power]

**Infrastructure challenges:**
- Poor/very poor roads (20–40% quality); low electricity access (<50%); customs delays (72–120+ hrs, unreliable)
- High ambient temperature (35–45°C daytime); long transit; remote endpoints (no grid, minimal facilities)
- Weak institutional capacity; corruption/customs inefficiency; security concerns on some routes

**Equipment specification:**

| Component | Technology | Rationale | Cost |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Transport container** | **Passive insulated box + PCM packs (2–3 backup sets); high-R insulation (80–100mm foam); vacuum/double-wall construction** OR **Solar-powered cooler (truck-mounted, 1,000–2,000 L; primary transport)** | Passive alone insufficient for 3–5 day/120+ hr routes in high heat; solar-powered vehicle is workhorse for this tier; 100% passive as backup | $600–900 (passive ultra-insulated); $8,000–12,000 (solar truck cooler) |
| **Temperature monitoring** | Data logger + GPS tracker (vehicle-mounted); 2 per shipment (redundancy); SMS/satellite uplink (in case cellular unavailable) | Satellite uplink for remote routes where cellular absent; GPS tracks vehicle location (verify customs delays, identify bottlenecks) | $300–400 per logger; $200–300 per GPS unit |
| **Depot storage** | Standalone freezer (grid optional) OR **solar-powered refrigerator + backup propane/kerosene unit** | No reliable grid in Tier 3 areas; solar + backup fuel essential; propane system for outages (e.g., Dometic-style hybrid fridge) | $3,000–5,000 (solar fridge + backup) |
| **Solar infrastructure at depot** | 5–10 kW solar array + lithium battery bank (50–100 kWh); pure sine-wave inverter; charge controller | Sunny regions (Sahel, East Africa highlands) have excellent solar resource (5–6 kWh/m²/day); supports refrigerator + ice maker + charging for vehicle coolers | $15,000–25,000 |
| **In-transit backup** | Spare PCM/ice (4–5 sets for 5-day trip); emergency coolers (styrofoam + wet burlap—low-tech passive) | Multiple redundancy essential; emergency coolers are ultra-low-cost ($20) backup if primary fails | $150–250 per shipment (consumables) |
| **Last-mile transport & storage** | **Ultra-passive "vaccine carriers" (insulated small boxes, 10–20L, designed for 8–24 hr hold without recharge) + ice packs; OR battery-operated small coolers (12V, solar-charged weekly at depot)** | Most remote health centers have no power; ultra-passive is fail-safe; battery coolers for monthly supply runs (larger centers) | $200–350 (passive carrier); $1,200–2,000 (battery cooler + solar panel) |
| **Health center storage** | Passive insulated cabinet (ultra-simple, single or dual compartment) + ice packs (replenished weekly by health worker or monthly by technician) | No electricity available; design is ultra-simple (no moving parts, easy to use with minimal training) | $250–400 per cabinet |

**Process & staffing:**

- **In-transit (solar vehicle):** 1 driver + 1 cold-chain monitor + 1 security/navigator (route safety); daily check-ins at fixed points (GPS logs + temp photo); route optimized for rest stops (avoid overheating vehicle)
- **Customs:** Pre-positioned expeditor at key borders; bonding agreement to reduce dwell time to <48 hrs; if delay unavoidable, use powered cooling at checkpoint or advance shipment to next depot
- **Depot staff:** 1 technician (lead) + 1 assistant; solar system maintenance (panel cleaning, battery monitoring); ice production; vaccine storage
- **Last-mile:** Community health worker (trained on passive carrier, ice replacement) + monthly district technician visit (supply, training, maintenance)

**Spoilage risk mitigation:**

| Risk | Mitigation |
|---|---|
| **Customs delay (120+ hrs) | Solar-powered vehicle cooler primary strategy; pre-clearance/bonding to minimize; if delay >48 hrs, escalate (move to larger powered depot or trigger emergency supply route) |
| **High ambient heat (35–45°C)** | Redundant PCM/ice; ultra-insulated passive boxes; solar cooler on vehicle; drive at night if possible (lower ambient) |
| **Road damage & temperature cycling** | Tough containers (no glass; minimal openings); backup cooling mandatory; expect 5–8°C temperature swings; redundant monitoring |
| **No grid at remote endpoints** | Pure passive system for health centers; monthly supply run (adequate if ice/PCM refreshed weekly); no expectation of powered storage at endpoint |
| **Staff turnover & training gaps** | Ultra-simple carrier design (minimal training needed); laminated instructions (diagrams, no text if literacy low); monthly site visit by technician (hands-on coaching) |
| **Vehicle breakdown** | Solar vehicle as redundancy (2 vehicles per route if possible); emergency passive box transfer (quickly switchable); spare parts pre-positioned along route |

**Network design:**
- Hub: Ouagadougou (WA-3), Yaoundé (WA-4), remote Dar or regional center (EA-3)
- 2–3 regional "mini-depots" (solar-powered, passive backup) every 300–400 km along main corridor
- 5–8 district-level distribution points (some powered via solar, some passive-only)
- Health centers: served by mobile team (monthly supply run) + emergency re-supply (2–week buffer at health center)

**Special feature: Mobile solar-powered vaccine clinic**
- Solar-powered truck + refrigeration + portable vaccination station
- Travels corridor monthly; brings vaccines to health centers; collects cold-chain data; trains staff
- Extends reach to remote areas without fixed infrastructure; builds capacity

**Financial model:**
- Capital: $60K–100K per hub (solar + redundant backup); $20K–35K per regional mini-depot; $3K–5K per health center passive cabinet; $50K–80K per mobile clinic vehicle
- Operating cost: $0.25–0.40 per dose (fuel for solar vehicle, ice/PCM, technician time, maintenance, redundancy buffer)
- Spoilage rate target: 2–3% (solar + monitoring + ultra-redundancy + buffer stock)

---

##### TIER 4 (Emergency/Seasonal) Supply Routes

**Scenario:** Remote node (300+ km, no road, 10+ day delivery); seasonal access only (rainy season closure); emergency restock (disease outbreak).

**Equipment specification (ultra-minimal):**

| Component | Technology | Rationale |
|---|---|---|
| **Transport** | Motorcycle, bicycle, or foot courier (if no vehicle access); **motorcycle with 20–30L insulated sidebox + PCM packs** | Vehicle choice determined by terrain; motorcycle most practical for rough paths |
| **Container** | Ultra-insulated 5–10L box (vacuum-insulated or double-walled foam); PCM (3–4 packs); 2–3 spare packs | <5L per day supply for remote clinic; passive hold 2–3 days if sealed well |
| **Monitoring** | Min/max thermometer (analog, no battery required); temperature log sheet (paper) | Cellular/GPS not available; manual logging on arrival at endpoint |
| **Backup** | Paper ice—wrap vaccine in damp cloth inside insulated bag if no ice available (emergency fallback; reduces thermal cycling) | Extremely low-cost (<$0) emergency measure if ice/PCM exhausted |
| **Health center storage** | Shaded, insulated box (no power) with ice/PCM packs replaced every 3 days | Passive only; expect 5–10°C variance; weekly inventory pull to minimize hold time |

**Frequency:** Quarterly or as-needed (emergency); not routine supply chain (too risky for regular distribution).

**Spoilage risk mitigation:** Pre-position 4-week buffer stock before rainy season closure; emergency supply only if outbreak/critical shortage; accept higher spoilage risk (5–10%) for remote areas.

---

### B. Phased Rollout Plan (24 Months)

**Logic:** Prove system on mature corridors first; scale to challenging corridors; iterate and optimize.

#### Phase 1: Pilot & Prove (Months 1–6)

**Objective:** Validate equipment, processes, and partnership model on Tier 1 corridor; establish baseline; train initial team.

**Focus: WA-1 (Senegal→Mali) OR EA-1 (Kenya→Uganda)**

**Rationale for WA-1 choice:** Lowest complexity; existing relationship with Senegal MoH; good road/customs baseline; can scale to Mali.

**Rollout steps:**

1. **Week 1–2: Site selection & baseline audit**
   - Identify Dakar hub, 2 regional depots (Kayes, Ségou, Mali), 5 district centers
   - Audit current cold-chain: equipment, temperature logs, spoilage rates, staff training
   - Document baseline: expected ~5% spoilage, ~75% on-time delivery, high error rates in manual logging

2. **Week 2–4: Procurement & equipment delivery**
   - Order: 3 passive containers, 1 powered cooler, 5 data loggers, 1 solar UPS for hub, basic tools
   - Lead time: 4–6 weeks from vendor; arrange local assembly/installation support

3. **Week 3–8: Partnership & training setup**
   - Bilateral agreement with Mali MoH: define roles, SLAs, data-sharing protocols
   - Recruit/assign cold-chain technician at each depot (5 people); 1 week training (hands-on + theory)
   - Train drivers (2 per major route) on vehicle inspection, temperature monitoring, emergency procedures
   - Health center staff (10 people across 5 centers): 2-day training on passive container, temperature logging, inventory management
